File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-31718", "CVE-2022-20210")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-31718", "CVE-2022-20210")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",

status: experimental

    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

Bulk cadastral record enumeration/scraping from DGFiP SPDC portal (apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single web session/source IP fetching an anomalously large number of distinct cadastral records from the French tax authority's Serveur Professionnel de Données Cadastrales (apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr). This is the exact behaviour ZeroBytes described — automated scraping that pulled 252,149 records / ~2M property holders over an extended period. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated SPDC host apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr (the pre-extracted IOC 'apexappliexi.dgfp...' is a corrupted spelling) and ZeroBytes' own account of scraping 252,149 records. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: this is server-side portal-log volumetrics that endpoint EDR and AWS trails cannot observe. Sigma skipped — it's a per-window distinct-count threshold, not single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-tax-authority-data-breach-affects-678-000-individuals/ • https://cyberinsider.com/french-tax-agency-confirms-breach-as-hacker-claims-2-million-victims/ • https://www.cyberattaque.org/dgfip-2-cyberattaque-cadastre/ • https://therecord.media/french-tax-authority-dgfip-confirms-data-breach
ATT&CKT1213 T1119
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Notary/surveyor firm running a large legitimate batch of cadastral lookups for a municipal project
  • Authorized DGFiP ETL/data-migration job pulling records from SPDC
  • Internal QA or load-testing generating high request volume against the portal
  • A monitoring/uptime crawler or search indexer hitting many URLs
  • A power user paginating through hundreds of parcels for a large land-transaction case
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))   // scraping came from an external actor; drops internal ETL/QA jobs
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull SrcIpAddr/SrcUsername and SampleUrls; confirm whether the account is a provisioned SPDC professional and whether the ASN/user-agent match known-good. Look for sequential/incrementing record IDs indicating automated enumeration. Step 2 (contain): If unauthorized, disable and rotate the SPDC account, terminate active sessions, and block the source IP/ASN at the WAF fronting apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr. Step 3 (hunt): Sum total distinct records touched by that IP/account over the full lookback to scope exposure, pivot the IP across other DGFiP hosts, and check whether the same IP authenticated to additional accounts.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowHours = 1h;
let DistinctRecordThreshold = 200;   // 200 distinct record URLs/hr per source far exceeds a
                                     // notaire's manual lookups; ZeroBytes scraped 252,149 records
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where HttpHostName has "apexappliext" or Url has "apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr"
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200", "206")   // successful record fetches
| summarize DistinctRecords = dcount(Url),
            TotalRequests = count(),
            SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 5),
            UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowHours)
| where DistinctRecords > DistinctRecordThreshold
| order by DistinctRecords desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Stolen DGFiP SPDC account used from multiple source IPs (valid-account + MFA-bypass access) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single authenticated user of the SPDC cadastral portal (apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr) appearing from several distinct source IPs in a short window — the fingerprint of ZeroBytes' claimed access via a stolen valid account and MFA bypass, holding the session over an extended period. Distinct pivot from the volumetric-scraping UC: it keys on account-from-many-origins rather than request volume. Rationale: Uses the corroborated SPDC host and the multi-source confirmation that access came from a stolen valid account with MFA bypass. Endpoint/cloud queries left empty — the authentication was against a bespoke French government web portal whose logs land in WAF/proxy/IIS, not Entra SigninLogs, Defender, or AWS CloudTrail. Sigma skipped: distinct-count aggregation over a time window, not single-event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberattaque.org/dgfip-2-cyberattaque-cadastre/ • https://cyberinsider.com/french-tax-agency-confirms-breach-as-hacker-claims-2-million-victims/ • https://cryptoast.fr/france-2-millions-de-proprietaires-vises-par-une-nouvelle-fuite-a-la-dgfip/
ATT&CKT1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A notaire accessing the portal from office, home, and mobile networks in the same day
  • Corporate NAT/proxy egress rotating multiple public IPs for one user
  • VPN split-tunnel or reconnection changing the source IP mid-session
  • A shared professional/service account legitimately used by a team from several locations
  • Carrier-grade NAT on mobile connections rotating the observed source IP
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Enumerate the distinct source IPs/ASNs for the flagged account and geolocate them; flag any hosting/VPS/foreign IPs that don't match the professional's registered location or usual egress. Step 2 (contain): Force a credential reset and MFA re-enrolment for the account and invalidate all active sessions to the SPDC portal. Step 3 (hunt): Check whether the suspicious IPs also touched other SPDC accounts (credential-theft spread), and cross-reference with the bulk-enumeration UC to see if any of these sessions performed high-volume record scraping.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let WindowHours = 24h;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where HttpHostName has "apexappliext" or Url has "apexappliext.dgfip.finances.gouv.fr"
| where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
| summarize DistinctSourceIPs = dcount(SrcIpAddr),
            SourceIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20),
            Requests = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowHours)
| where DistinctSourceIPs >= 3   // one cadastral account from 3+ IPs/day = credential sharing/theft;
                                 // ZeroBytes used a stolen valid account + MFA bypass to hold access
| order by DistinctSourceIPs desc

Evooo1Bot loader retrieval — connection to hardcoded loader host 91.92.40.118 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts any host establishing a connection to the Evooo1Bot loader server 91.92.40.118, which hosts wget.sh and 12 architecture-specific ELF payloads. All Fortinet-observed payload callbacks pointed to this single IP, making it a high-fidelity network IOC for the delivery stage. Rationale: 91.92.40.118 is the single hardcoded loader host all Evooo1Bot payload callbacks pointed to per Fortinet's telemetry; a direct IP IOC with essentially no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-evooo1bot-linux-botnet-turns-routers-into-traffic-relay-nodes/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/linux-botnet-evooo1bot-mirai-capabilities-beyond-ddos
ATT&CKT1105 T1584.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher/sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the IOC
  • VPN/NAT egress where an unrelated benign host shares the recorded source IP
  • Firewall block events (connection attempted but denied) inflating alert volume without a real infection
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm direction — was the connection allowed or blocked at the perimeter? Identify the internal host and the process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) that reached out. 2) Contain: block 91.92.40.118 at the firewall/egress proxy and network-isolate the source host; on Linux edge devices assume full compromise. 3) Hunt: pivot to that host for wget.sh execution, /tmp ELF drops matching the known SHA256s, bash-history clearing, and outbound port-443 beacons or port-22 fan-out.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP == "91.92.40.118"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationIP == "91.92.40.118" or SourceIP == "91.92.40.118"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot wget.sh fetch-and-execute loader chain on Linux AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Evooo1Bot install chain where an exploited Linux host runs wget/curl to pull wget.sh from 91.92.40.118, then chmod +x and executes an architecture-matched ELF from /tmp. Targets the shell loader behaviour rather than a single IOC. Rationale: Combines the named loader script (wget.sh), the loader IP, and the Mirai-style /tmp ELF chmod+x behaviour Fortinet describes — three article-specific strings that together are high-fidelity for the install phase. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-evooo1bot-linux-botnet-turns-routers-into-traffic-relay-nodes/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin bootstrap scripts that curl an install shell and chmod +x binaries in /tmp
  • Configuration-management (Ansible/Salt) staging tooling into /tmp
  • CI/CD build agents downloading and marking test binaries executable
  • Package-manager wrappers that fetch install.sh from a vendor host (but not 91.92.40.118)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the downloaded URL/host — a hit on 91.92.40.118 or wget.sh is near-certain malicious; a bare chmod+x /tmp hit needs the parent process and download source checked. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, and remove the /tmp ELF; block 91.92.40.118. 3) Hunt: check for persistence (cron/rc.local/systemd), bash-history clearing, and outbound 443 C2 or port-22 brute-force fan-out from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("wget","curl") and ProcessCommandLine has "91.92.40.118")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "wget.sh"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "chmod" and ProcessCommandLine has "+x" and ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has "wget.sh"
    or (SyslogMessage has "91.92.40.118" and (SyslogMessage has "wget" or SyslogMessage has "curl"))
    or (SyslogMessage has "chmod" and SyslogMessage has "+x" and SyslogMessage has "/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot anti-forensics — bash history clearing after payload execution AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Evooo1Bot loader's trace-erasure step where it clears bash history (history -c, truncating ~/.bash_history to /dev/null, unsetting HISTFILE) immediately after fetching the botnet binary. Article-specific defense-evasion behaviour explicitly called out by Fortinet. Rationale: Fortinet explicitly notes the loader 'clears Bash history to erase traces'; the specific command variants (history -c, HISTFILE unset, ~/.bash_history to /dev/null) are the concrete anti-forensic strings this behaviour produces. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/evooo1bot-linux-botnet-exploits-known.html
ATT&CKT1070.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins clearing their own history for privacy/hygiene after typing secrets
  • Dotfile/shell-profile setups that unset HISTFILE in automation
  • Interactive troubleshooting sessions running history -c
  • Ephemeral container entrypoints that null out HISTFILE by design
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wget","curl","/tmp/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the history-clear with the same host/user's recent process tree — a clear that immediately follows a /tmp download or wget.sh is high-signal; a lone interactive clear by a known admin is likely benign. 2) Contain: if paired with loader/network IOCs, isolate the host and preserve /tmp and auditd logs before the actor removes more. 3) Hunt: look on the same host for the ELF drop (known SHA256s), 91.92.40.118 connections, and port-443 beaconing.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has ".bash_history" and (ProcessCommandLine has "/dev/null" or ProcessCommandLine has "rm " or ProcessCommandLine has "truncate"))
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "history" and ProcessCommandLine has "-c")
    or ProcessCommandLine has "unset HISTFILE"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "HISTFILE=/dev/null"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (SyslogMessage has ".bash_history" and (SyslogMessage has "/dev/null" or SyslogMessage has "rm " or SyslogMessage has "truncate"))
    or (SyslogMessage has "history" and SyslogMessage has "-c")
    or SyslogMessage has "unset HISTFILE"
    or SyslogMessage has "HISTFILE=/dev/null"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot ELF payload drop by known SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts creation/execution of the Evooo1Bot botnet binary using the two Fortinet-published SHA256 hashes. Direct file-hash IOC for the install stage across any Linux host with file/hash telemetry. Rationale: Two Fortinet-published SHA256 hashes for the Evooo1Bot binary — exact-match file IOCs with zero legitimate collision risk. Datadog left empty as auditd/syslog do not carry file hashes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://cybersecuritynews.com/evooo1bot-linux-botnet/
ATT&CKT1105 T1584.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis VM or sandbox storing the sample for research
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of the same file re-hashing
  • Threat-intel sharing repositories syncing the sample onto a fileserver
  • Reverse-engineering lab host intentionally holding the binary
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("malware-lab01","sandbox-vm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is not a sanctioned malware-analysis system; identify the writing/executing process and file path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and quarantine the ELF, and block 91.92.40.118. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same hashes and for the wget.sh loader chain, bash-history clearing, and 443 beaconing to find sibling infections.
union DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents

| where SHA256 in ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109","4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109","4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Evooo1Bot SSH brute-force scanner — outbound port-22 fan-out from a single host AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an infected edge device or server acting as the Evooo1Bot SSH brute-force scanner, generating outbound SSH connections to a large number of distinct destinations in a short window. Targets the worm/propagation behaviour rather than a single IOC. Rationale: Fortinet lists an integrated SSH brute-force scanner as a core Evooo1Bot module; a single host opening SSH to 50+ distinct destinations in a 10-minute window is the network fan-out signature that behaviour produces and is distinct from the IP/hash IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/multi-functional-linux-botnet-evooo1bot • https://www.darkreading.com/cyber-risk/linux-botnet-evooo1bot-mirai-capabilities-beyond-ddos
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) sweeping SSH across the estate
  • Ansible/config-management control node pushing to many managed Linux hosts
  • Backup or monitoring server that SSHes to a large host inventory
  • CI runner deploying to many targets over SSH
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","nessusd","qualys","scanner") and DeviceName !in~ ("ansible-ctl01","backup01","nagios01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and initiating process; confirm it is not a sanctioned scanner/automation node and whether targets are internal, external, or both. 2) Contain: isolate the host and block outbound port 22 from it at the firewall if it is not an authorized jump/automation host. 3) Hunt: on the source host look for the Evooo1Bot loader chain, known ELF hashes, and 91.92.40.118 connections; review target hosts for successful SSH logins indicating propagation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 22 and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(RemoteIP), Sample = make_set(RemoteIP, 20), Attempts = count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets > 50   // 50 distinct SSH targets in 10m = scanner-like fan-out, well above interactive admin use
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 22
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Sample = make_set(DestinationIP, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets > 50   // 50 distinct SSH targets in 10m = scanner fan-out
| order by DistinctTargets desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=22
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true))
| _count > 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=22 by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 50
| sort - distinct_targets
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as distinct_targets count from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=22 by All_Traffic.src_ip _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| where distinct_targets > 50
| sort - distinct_targets
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")

| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or SHA1 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or MD5 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or SHA1 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d") or MD5 in~ ("f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f13cb360768363d3424e2192c7805b8c8015eb8706dbbbcdead6aed8cf390109", "4c0886349e9d348569fffe1b7a31e474d514508bf0cd6f1e5dd99c2a73525e4d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Quishing delivery: inbound email with QR-code image/PDF attachment and no scannable body URL AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound emails whose only clickable destination is hidden inside a QR code embedded as an image (PNG/JPG/GIF/BMP/SVG) or PDF attachment, with zero URLs in the body — the exact evasion the article and the FBI Kimsuky FLASH alert describe (link concealed in a visual pattern so mail filters cannot extract and inspect it). Article-specific because it targets the QR-in-attachment shape, not a generic link-phish. Rationale: Uses the article's core evasion (link encoded only in a QR image inside a PDF/JPEG attachment, minimal body text) expressed as EmailAttachmentInfo image/PDF + UrlCount==0; cross-checked against the FBI FLASH alert (ic3.gov/CSA/2026/260108.pdf) and the documented EmailAttachmentInfo hunt pattern from Sonne's Cloud and Stripe OLT. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2026/260108.pdf • https://blog.sonnes.cloud/defender-for-office-365-hunting-and-responding-to-qr-code-based-phishing-attacks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/fbi-warns-north-korean-hackers-using.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vendor invoices/statements delivered as a single PDF with no body URL
  • Marketing or event emails that embed a genuine QR code (conference badge, restaurant menu, payment) as an inline image
  • Scanner/MFP 'scan-to-email' jobs that arrive as a lone image or PDF attachment with an empty body
  • Internal newsletters forwarded inbound from a partner tenant that render as image attachments
  • e-signature/DocuSign-style notifications that ship a PDF and place the action link behind a button rendered as an image
Suppression filter
| where not(SenderFromDomain in~ ("docusign.net","echosign.com","adobesign.com")) and not(Subject has_any ("scan from","scanned document","scan to email"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Decode the QR in the attachment (offline/sandboxed) to recover the destination URL; check the sender domain's SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails and whether the display name impersonates a trusted brand (DocuSign, Microsoft) or an advisor/embassy contact per the Kimsuky lures. 2) CONTAIN: If the decoded URL is malicious, soft-delete/purge the message from all recipient mailboxes (Explorer/AIR), block the sender and URL/domain, and warn recipients not to scan on personal phones. 3) HUNT: Pivot on SenderFromAddress and attachment SHA256 across the tenant for other recipients, then check UrlClickEvents and AADSignInEventsBeta for any recipient who authenticated shortly after (see the token-replay UC).
let lookback = 14d;
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where UrlCount == 0            // quishing hides the link inside the QR image, so the body carries no scannable URL
| where AttachmentCount between (1 .. 3)   // targeted lure, not a bulk newsletter with many images
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
    | extend Ext = tolower(extract(@"\.([^.]+)$", 1, FileName))
    | where Ext in ("png","jpg","jpeg","gif","bmp","svg","pdf")
    | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName, FileType, Ext, SHA256, FileSize
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, FileSize, SHA256,
          AuthenticationDetails, NetworkMessageId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let lookback = 14d;
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| where UrlCount == 0            // quishing hides the link inside the QR image, so the body carries no scannable URL
| where AttachmentCount between (1 .. 3)   // targeted lure, not a bulk newsletter with many images
| join kind=inner (
    EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)

    | where Ext in ("png","jpg","jpeg","gif","bmp","svg","pdf")

  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName, Ext, FileSize, SHA256,
          AuthenticationDetails, NetworkMessageId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Post-quishing cloud token replay: MFA-satisfied sign-in shortly after QR-attachment email AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a recipient of a QR-code attachment email with a subsequent successful Entra sign-in where MFA was satisfied without an interactive challenge (single-factor requirement / replayed session token) — the outcome the FBI FLASH alert calls out: session-token theft and replay that hijacks cloud identities 'without triggering typical MFA-failed alerts.' Article/campaign-specific via the email→identity join, not a generic risky-sign-in rule. Rationale: Anchors on the FBI-confirmed campaign outcome (session-token replay bypassing MFA without MFA-failed events) by joining QR-attachment recipients to same-user successful sign-ins where AuthenticationRequirement was singleFactor; Sentinel/Splunk fall back to identity-only rarity because the M365 Defender email tables (EmailEvents/EmailAttachmentInfo) are not in this tenant's listed Sentinel/CIM schema, so the email anchor is only fully expressible in Defender XDR. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2026/260108.pdf • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-warns-about-kimsuky-hackers-using-qr-codes-to-phish-us-orgs/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fbi-north-korean-spear-phishing-attacks-use-malicious-qr-codes/
ATT&CKT1550.004 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Road-warrior users signing in from a new hotel/airport IP while a valid session token is still alive (legitimate single-factor via SSO)
  • Conditional Access sessions where a trusted/compliant device legitimately satisfies auth without a new MFA prompt
  • Corporate VPN or ZTNA egress rotating to an IP not seen in the baseline window
  • Mobile app token refresh after a genuine QR/vendor email the user happened to receive that day
  • New corporate proxy or ISP block introduced during the baseline gap causing benign leftanti hits
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName == "" or isempty(DeviceName)   // drop sign-ins from managed/compliant devices where token reuse is expected; keep unmanaged-device replays
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in has no matching interactive MFA event and originates from an IP/device new to the user; correlate the join'd QR-attachment email and decode its QR destination to check for an AiTM/credential-harvest page. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset, require re-registration of phishing-resistant MFA, and block the source IP/ASN. 3) HUNT: Review the account for post-auth mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, and access to SharePoint/Exchange from the same session; expand to other QR-attachment recipients from the same sender for additional token-replay sign-ins.
let lookback = 14d;
let CorrelationWindow = 24h;
let QuishingRecipients =
    EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered" and UrlCount == 0
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailAttachmentInfo
        | extend Ext = tolower(extract(@"\.([^.]+)$", 1, FileName))
        | where Ext in ("png","jpg","jpeg","gif","bmp","svg","pdf")
        | project NetworkMessageId, AttachmentName = FileName
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | project EmailTime = Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, AttachmentName;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication"   // token/claim satisfied auth with no interactive MFA — replay hallmark
| join kind=inner QuishingRecipients on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| where Timestamp between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + CorrelationWindow)
| project SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City,
          Application, DeviceName, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, RiskState,
          EmailTime, Subject, AttachmentName
| order by SignInTime desc
let lookback = 14d;
let baseline = 30d;
let KnownIPs = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(baseline) .. ago(lookback))
    | where ResultType == 0
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationRequirement == "singleFactorAuthentication"   // MFA satisfied by existing token/claim, not an interactive prompt
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("medium","high")
| join kind=leftanti KnownIPs on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress       // IP never seen for this user during baseline

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspected China-Nexus Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw, Deploys Babuk-Derived Ransomware

The Hacker News
2026-08-17 19 use cases 5 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have attributed the exploitation of a newly patched security flaw in Broadcom VMware vCenter to a suspected China-nexus advanced persistent threat (APT). The attacks involve the exploitation of CVE-2026-59310 (CVSS score: 9.8), a severe directory-traversal vulnerability in the VMware vCenter server that could be weaponized by a malicious actor to execute arbitrary code

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Rogue vSphere admin account creation via GoodMoodle-VCFleet UA from 146.59.252.178 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vCenter CVE-2026-59310 PoC cron drop + backdoor fetch (zz-poc59310-syslog.log) · [LLM] Passwordless root sudoers grant for perfcharts (/etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf) · [LLM] vmdir credential theft via /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh and vmafd module · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Suspected China-Nexus Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw, Deploys Babuk-Derived
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] VMware-impersonating cron jobs drop JSP webshell (vmware-perf-update.jsp) · [LLM] esxi.sh downloader deploys architecture-specific reverse_ssh from 185.144.28.120
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] linuxFile backdoor WebSocket C2 to intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop and campaign C2 IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Babuk-derived .babyk ransomware encryption on ESXi hosts · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
vCenter CVE-2026-59310 PoC cron drop + backdoor fetch (zz-poc59310-syslog.log) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-59310 exploitation footprint on VMware vCSA: a malformed cron file named 'zz-poc59310-syslog.log' written under /etc/cron.d followed by a curl/wget retrieving the 'linuxFile' backdoor from 5.34.177[.]38:9861. Article-specific because the filename literally references the CVE PoC and the C2 host is fixed infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the fixed PoC-derived filename 'zz-poc59310-syslog.log' in the privileged /etc/cron.d location plus the hardcoded backdoor host 5.34.177[.]38:9861 — both unique to this campaign and unlikely to appear benignly.
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate vCSA syslog rotation writing *.log to the configured syslog output dir (not /etc/cron.d)
  • Broadcom-supplied cron jobs under /etc/cron.d during patching
  • Security scanner staging a benign PoC test file during authorized vuln validation
  • Backup agent temp-writing to /etc/cron.d
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d" and FileName has_any ("poc59310","zz-poc59310-syslog.log")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the exact cron file contents and the crond/auditd log line; confirm the file is under /etc/cron.d (not the syslog output dir) and whether cron executed it (look for the follow-on curl/wget to 5.34.177[.]38:9861). 2) Contain: isolate the vCSA appliance from network, block egress to 5.34.177[.]38 and the other C2 IPs, snapshot for forensics, and disable/rotate any vCenter admin credentials. 3) Hunt: search all vCSA hosts for the linuxFile backdoor, systemd persistence, and other cron files named vmware-perf-*/vmware-vpxd-stats-* and connections to intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d" and (FileName =~ "zz-poc59310-syslog.log" or FileName has "poc59310")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| union (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("curl","wget")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "5.34.177.38" or ProcessCommandLine has ":9861"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType = "BackdoorFetch", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName = AccountName
)
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "zz-poc59310" or SyslogMessage has "poc59310-syslog"
    or (SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget") and (SyslogMessage has "5.34.177.38" or SyslogMessage has ":9861"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

linuxFile backdoor WebSocket C2 to intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop and campaign C2 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts egress from a compromised vCSA/ESXi host to the 'linuxFile' implant controller at ws://intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop:8080/ws and the campaign's fixed C2/staging IPs. Article-specific because these are named C2 endpoints for a WebSocket-over-ws:// implant with app-layer crypto. Rationale: Pivots on the exact implant controller domain intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop:8080/ws and the five fixed campaign C2/staging IPs — high-fidelity network IOCs tied to the linuxFile WebSocket backdoor.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/EDR sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate egress IP
  • Security researcher connecting to the C2 for analysis
  • Shared-hosting IP later reassigned to a benign service (recheck IP reputation age)
  • Firewall log replay/testing re-ingesting historical IOC traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the source host — a WebSocket connection from a vCSA process to intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop:8080 is the linuxFile implant; capture the process tree and binary hash. 2) Contain: null-route/block all five C2 IPs and the domain at the perimeter, isolate the source host, and preserve the implant binary and systemd unit. 3) Hunt: sweep for the implant's systemd/cron persistence, the reverse_ssh binary, JSP webshells, and any of the rogue accounts (vcenter_admin, adminuser, vcadmin, perfcharts) across the estate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop"
    or RemoteIP in ("5.34.177.38","185.144.28.120","192.255.141.13","5.34.176.100","146.59.252.178")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2ips = dynamic(["5.34.177.38","185.144.28.120","192.255.141.13","5.34.176.100","146.59.252.178"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationIP in (c2ips) or DestinationHostName has "intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop"
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceProduct),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has "se9ly9upbhay.shop"
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VMware-impersonating cron jobs drop JSP webshell (vmware-perf-update.jsp) AIInstallation High
Hunts the attacker's persistence cron jobs masquerading as VMware services (vmware-vpxd-stats-*, vmware-perf-collect-*, vmware-perf-sync-*) and the JSP webshell they drop, 'vmware-perf-update.jsp'. Article-specific because the cron-name pattern and webshell filename are unique lures mimicking legitimate vCenter perfcharts components. Rationale: The webshell name 'vmware-perf-update.jsp' and the three attacker cron prefixes (vmware-vpxd-stats-/vmware-perf-collect-/vmware-perf-sync-) are lures unique to this actor mimicking vCenter perfcharts — legitimate vCenter does not drop JSP files by these names under /etc/cron.d.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1053.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine vCenter perfcharts application updates writing .jsp under the Tomcat webapps dir (not the attacker's path/name)
  • Broadcom patch installing legitimately-named vmware-* cron jobs
  • Admin manually staging a support-bundle script named similarly
  • Backup restore replaying historical files
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the JSP webshell contents and the cron job body; confirm whether the cron adds an SSH key (vmware-vpxd-stats), drops the webshell (vmware-perf-collect), or runs the base64 credential-access script and creates 'adminuser' (vmware-perf-sync). 2) Contain: remove the cron files and webshell, isolate the appliance, and revoke/rotate vSphere SSO admin credentials and the 'adminuser' account. 3) Hunt: check authorized_keys for attacker keys, look for the /etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf sudoers grant and /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh, and correlate with C2 to intel.se9ly9upbhay.shop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "vmware-perf-update.jsp"
    or (FolderPath has "/etc/cron.d" and FileName has_any ("vmware-vpxd-stats-","vmware-perf-collect-","vmware-perf-sync-"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "vmware-perf-update.jsp"
    or SyslogMessage has_any ("vmware-vpxd-stats-","vmware-perf-collect-","vmware-perf-sync-")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Passwordless root sudoers grant for perfcharts (/etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf) AIExploitation High
Hunts creation of /etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf granting the 'perfcharts' service account unrestricted, non-interactive (NOPASSWD) sudo to root on vCSA. Article-specific because the exact sudoers filename and the perfcharts principal are the actor's privilege-escalation mechanism. Rationale: The exact sudoers drop path /etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf combined with the perfcharts principal and NOPASSWD:ALL is the actor's precise privesc artifact — no legitimate VMware process grants perfcharts passwordless root.
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1098
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Broadcom installer adding a legitimately-named sudoers file (not 'vmware-perf' with perfcharts NOPASSWD)
  • Sysadmin manually editing sudoers.d during troubleshooting
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Salt) pushing a sudoers template
  • Support-bundle tooling temporarily elevating a service account
Suppression filter
| where FileName =~ "vmware-perf" and FolderPath has "/etc/sudoers.d"
Response runbook
1) Triage: cat /etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf and confirm it grants perfcharts NOPASSWD:ALL; check file owner/mtime and the process that created it. 2) Contain: delete the sudoers file, lock the perfcharts account, isolate the appliance, and audit for any commands already run as root via that grant. 3) Hunt: look for the paired /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh credential-theft script, vmdir registry queries, the adminuser/vcadmin accounts, and C2 beacons to confirm full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/etc/sudoers.d" and FileName =~ "vmware-perf"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/etc/sudoers.d/vmware-perf"
    or (SyslogMessage has "perfcharts" and SyslogMessage has "NOPASSWD")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
