vmdir credential theft via /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh and vmafd module AIExploitation High
Hunts the actor's credential-access script (/tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh) that harvests vCenter machine-account credentials by querying the vmdir registry key HKEY_THIS_MACHINE\services\vmdir or, on failure, invoking VMware's vmafd Python module (GetMachineName/GetMachinePassword/GetDomainName). Article-specific: the hidden script path and these exact vmafd calls are the campaign's vmdir credential-dumping routine. Rationale: The hidden script path /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh plus the specific vmafd credential API calls (GetMachineName/GetMachinePassword/GetDomainName) and the vmdir registry key are the actor's precise vmdir credential-dumping technique, not normal vCenter operation.
ATT&CKT1003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VMware support scripts legitimately calling vmafd GetMachineName during appliance diagnostics
  • vdcadmintool/vmdir maintenance run by an admin during domain repair
  • Backup/DR tooling reading machine credentials during appliance re-registration
  • Broadcom KB remediation script referencing the vmdir service key
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the invoking user/parent for /tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh and whether vmafd machine-password calls succeeded; treat any success as vmdir machine-account compromise. 2) Contain: rotate the vCenter machine account and SSO admin credentials, isolate the appliance, and review vmdir for unauthorized 'adminuser'/'vcadmin' additions to the Administrators group. 3) Hunt: pivot to the LDAP Add operations against vmdir, the sudoers grant, and reverse_ssh/esxi.sh deployment to scope lateral movement to ESXi.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"services\vmdir"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("GetMachinePassword","GetMachineName","GetDomainName")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/tmp/.vmware-perf-upd.sh"
    or SyslogMessage has "services\\vmdir"
    or SyslogMessage has_any ("GetMachinePassword","GetMachineName","GetDomainName")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rogue vSphere admin account creation via GoodMoodle-VCFleet UA from 146.59.252.178 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-59309 auth-bypass abuse: vSphere REST API access using the masquerading User-Agent 'GoodMoodle-VCFleet/1.0' and/or activity from 146.59.252[.]178 that creates rogue admin accounts (vcenter_admin, adminuser, vcadmin). Article-specific because the UA string, source IP, and account names are all fixed campaign artifacts. Rationale: The User-Agent 'GoodMoodle-VCFleet/1.0' (deliberate masquerade of VCF Fleet), source IP 146.59.252[.]178, and rogue account names vcenter_admin/adminuser/vcadmin are fixed, campaign-unique artifacts of the CVE-2026-59309 auth-bypass phase.
ATT&CKT1078.003 T1136.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine VCF Fleet management traffic using the real product User-Agent (note the attacker UA is a near-miss masquerade — verify exact string)
  • Internal vulnerability scanner probing vCenter REST API from an allow-listed IP
  • Broadcom-hosted telemetry or support connection sharing similar UA
  • Pen-test engagement replicating the campaign UA with authorization
Suppression filter
| where http_user_agent="GoodMoodle-VCFleet/1.0" or src="146.59.252.178"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all vCenter REST/vpxd access log lines with UA GoodMoodle-VCFleet/1.0 or from 146.59.252[.]178; identify which admin account was used and what accounts were created. 2) Contain: block 146.59.252[.]178 at the perimeter, disable the rogue accounts (vcenter_admin, adminuser, vcadmin) and remove them from vSphere SSO Administrators, and force re-auth of legitimate admins. 3) Hunt: because no legitimate login preceded the account creation, review vmdir LDAP Add operations and the CVE-2026-59310 chain (cron backdoor, C2) on the same appliance.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "146.59.252.178" or LocalIP == "146.59.252.178"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
(union isfuzzy=true
  (Syslog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where SyslogMessage has "GoodMoodle-VCFleet" or SyslogMessage has "146.59.252.178"
       or SyslogMessage has_any ("vcenter_admin","adminuser","vcadmin")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where RequestClientApplication has "GoodMoodle-VCFleet" or SourceIP == "146.59.252.178"
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, RequestMethod))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

esxi.sh downloader deploys architecture-specific reverse_ssh from 185.144.28.120 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts cron-driven execution of 'esxi.sh' fetched from 185.144.28[.]120:3232 that installs an architecture-specific 'reverse_ssh' reverse-shell client, plus staging pulls from 192.255.141[.]13:8080 and the AList-exposed toolset at 5.34.176[.]100:5244. Article-specific because esxi.sh, reverse_ssh, and these staging endpoints are the campaign's lateral-movement-to-ESXi tooling. Rationale: esxi.sh and the reverse_ssh client name, together with the three fixed staging IPs (185.144.28[.]120:3232, 192.255.141[.]13:8080, 5.34.176[.]100:5244 — the last exposing the toolset via AList), are campaign-specific download-and-persist artifacts for reaching ESXi.
ATT&CKT1105 T1572 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin script coincidentally named esxi.sh for ESXi maintenance (verify content and source IP)
  • Authorized reverse-tunnel tooling (e.g. sanctioned SSH jump) matching 'reverse_ssh'
  • Config-management fetching ESXi patches from an internal mirror (not the campaign IPs)
  • IOC-list ingestion test replaying historical curl commands
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent cron job and whether esxi.sh downloaded/chmod+x'd a reverse_ssh binary; capture the binary and the destination staging directory. 2) Contain: block 185.144.28[.]120, 192.255.141[.]13, and 5.34.176[.]100, isolate the appliance, kill any reverse_ssh process, and check ESXi hosts for the 'adminuser' local account. 3) Hunt: enumerate ESXi hosts for local account creation and .babyk ransomware staging, and correlate with the linuxFile C2 and vmdir credential theft to scope the full intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "esxi.sh"
    or FileName =~ "reverse_ssh" or ProcessCommandLine has "reverse_ssh"
    or (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("185.144.28.120","192.255.141.13","5.34.176.100"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "esxi.sh" or SyslogMessage has "reverse_ssh"
    or SyslogMessage has_any ("185.144.28.120","192.255.141.13","5.34.176.100")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Babuk-derived .babyk ransomware encryption on ESXi hosts AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the campaign's terminal impact: mass file encryption on ESXi hosts appending the '.babyk' extension (Babuk-derived ransomware), often preceded by attacker-created local ESXi accounts (e.g. 'adminuser'). Article-specific because '.babyk' is the fixed ransomware marker for this Babuk-derived payload on ESXi. Rationale: The '.babyk' extension is the concrete, fixed marker of this Babuk-derived ESXi ransomware; a burst threshold (>20 encrypted files) separates true mass-encryption from an incidental filename and keeps the alert high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1486 T1136.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A single legitimately-named backup/archive file coincidentally ending in .babyk (threshold suppresses)
  • Malware-analysis lab intentionally detonating the sample on an isolated ESXi host
  • Restore of previously-encrypted files during recovery testing re-triggering file events
  • Security tool quarantining .babyk artifacts, generating file-rename events
Suppression filter
| where EncryptedFiles > 20
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the burst of .babyk files is on a production ESXi datastore and identify the encrypting process/account (check for attacker-created local ESXi account 'adminuser'). 2) Contain: power off / isolate affected ESXi hosts from management and storage networks to halt encryption, preserve unencrypted VMs and snapshots, and disable the rogue local accounts. 3) Hunt: trace back the intrusion chain — reverse_ssh/esxi.sh deployment, vmdir credential theft, and linuxFile C2 — to identify patient-zero vCSA and ensure CVE-2026-59310/59309 are patched (Broadcom fix 2026-07-29) across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".babyk" or ActionType == "FileRenamed" and FileName endswith ".babyk"
| summarize EncryptedFiles = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFile = any(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where EncryptedFiles > 20   // 20 = burst threshold to separate mass-encryption from a stray file
| order by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has ".babyk"
| summarize Hits = count(), Sample = any(SyslogMessage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, ProcessName
| where Hits > 20   // 20 = burst threshold for mass-encryption on an ESXi host
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Babuk-Derived .babyk Ransomware File Encryption on ESXi

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-59310", "CVE-2026-59309")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SafePal breach phishing wave: impersonation email with firmware-update / seed-phrase lure AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound email that impersonates SafePal following the Aug 2026 order-data breach, using the article's specific social-engineering theme (SafePal X1 firmware upgrade / verify identity / seed-phrase). Flags mail that references SafePal branding or the confirmed phishing domain safepal.support but does NOT originate from the legitimate safepal.com domain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact lure theme (SafePal X1 firmware-update-required / seed-phrase / verify-identity) plus the corroborated phishing domain safepal.support, anchored against the legit safepal.com sender domain so it only fires on impersonation, not real SafePal mail. Cross-checked against: • https://news.bitcoin.com/security/data-breach-hits-39798-safepal-customers-after-order-plugin-flaw/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197391/data-breach/safepal-says-39798-customers-hit-by-data-breach.html • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/cybersecurity-threats/news-safepal-data-breach-40000-customers/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SafePal marketing/newsletter sent via a third-party ESP domain that references SafePal branding but isn't safepal.com
  • News/security vendors emailing internal staff about the breach itself, quoting 'SafePal' and 'firmware' in the subject
  • Authorized security-awareness phishing simulations using a crypto-wallet lure template
  • Legitimate shipping/logistics partner order-update mail referencing the SafePal order but from a courier domain
  • Internal SOC threat-intel distribution lists forwarding the phishing sample for analysis
Suppression filter
| where DeliveryAction != "Blocked" and RecipientEmailAddress !endswith "@yourorg-secops.example" and SenderFromDomain !in~ ("knowbe4.com", "phishsim.yourorg.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full message via NetworkMessageId — inspect SenderMailFromDomain vs SenderFromDomain for spoofing, SPF/DKIM/DMARC in AuthenticationDetails, and whether any URL resolves to safepal.support or a safepal-lookalike. Confirm the recipient is a real SafePal customer/target. 2) Contain: If confirmed malicious, purge from all mailboxes (Explorer/soft-delete), block the sender domain and any lookalike URL domains at the mail gateway and web proxy, and warn recipients NOT to enter seed phrases/firmware. 3) Hunt: Run UC2 to see if any recipient's device already reached safepal.support or a lookalike; check UrlClickEvents for ClickAllowed/ClickedThrough on those URLs and pivot to any subsequent credential-entry or wallet activity.

Endpoint traffic to SafePal phishing site safepal.support / lookalike domains AIExploitation High
Hunts DNS/web egress from managed endpoints to the confirmed SafePal breach phishing domain safepal.support and other safepal-containing lookalikes that are NOT the official safepal.com. A hit means a user reached the seed-phrase-harvesting landing page — the credential-access stage of this campaign. Rationale: Anchored on the second-source-confirmed phishing domain safepal.support and a broad safepal-lookalike DNS match with the official safepal.com carved out, so any hit is high-fidelity evidence a user reached the credential/seed-phrase harvesting page. Cross-checked against: • https://news.bitcoin.com/security/data-breach-hits-39798-safepal-customers-after-order-plugin-flaw/ • https://securityaffairs.com/197391/data-breach/safepal-says-39798-customers-hit-by-data-breach.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/threat-intel analyst manually browsing safepal.support to triage the phishing page
  • Security proxy or sandbox appliance auto-detonating/scanning the URL from a scanning host
  • URL-reputation or DLP crawler resolving safepal-lookalike domains for classification
  • Coincidental non-malicious domain that merely contains the substring 'safepal' (e.g. an unrelated project/vanity host)
  • SafePal legitimate regional/CDN subdomain that does not end in safepal.com (verify ownership before dismissing)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox01", "urlscan-host01") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "brave.exe", "opera.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the device/user and the exact domain hit; confirm resolution succeeded and whether an HTTP session followed (pivot InitiatingProcessFileName — a browser vs. a script/LOLBin changes severity). Validate the domain is not a legitimate SafePal-owned host. 2) Contain: Block the domain and its resolved IP at proxy/firewall/DNS sinkhole, isolate the device if a credential-entry page was reached, and force the user to treat any SafePal wallet as compromised — advise immediate asset transfer to a new wallet per SafePal guidance. 3) Hunt: Search all endpoints for other safepal-lookalike resolutions, correlate to UC1 inbound phishing mail on the same user, and review browser/credential-store activity plus any clipboard/seed-phrase exposure in the window after the visit.

title: DNS Query to SafePal Breach Phishing Domain (safepal.support / lookalike)
id: 6b2f1c9a-3d47-4e2a-9c81-7a5e0b4f2d13
status: experimental
description: Detects DNS resolution of safepal-branded domains that are not the official safepal.com, tied to the Aug 2026 SafePal data-breach phishing wave (confirmed domain safepal.support).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/safepal-data-breach-impacts-39-798-customers-stolen-info-for-sale/
  - https://news.bitcoin.com/security/data-breach-hits-39798-safepal-customers-after-order-plugin-flaw/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/18
tags:
  - attack.t1566.002
  - attack.t1656
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'safepal'
  filter_legit:
    query|contains: 'safepal.com'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Analysts detonating the phishing URL in a sandbox
  - URL reputation scanners resolving the domain
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:*safepal* AND -@DestinationHostname:*safepal.com*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/safepal/i
| NOT DomainName=/safepal\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*safepal*" NOT DNS.query="*safepal.com*" by DNS.query DNS.src DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution where DNS.query="*safepal*" NOT DNS.query="*safepal.com*" by DNS.query DNS.src DNS.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | sort - lastTime
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] AmnesiaStealer ClickFix loader: macOS shell fetching payload from fake-GitHub / Amnesia C2 host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] AmnesiaStealer C2/relay egress to Amnesia Panel host (allllowef.space / aoitour.com) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AmnesiaStealer stream_module: headless Chromium launched with remote-debugging + hardening-off flags · [LLM] AmnesiaStealer credential harvest: keychain dump, APFS TCC-bypass mount, and fake password prompt · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AmnesiaStealer ClickFix loader: macOS shell fetching payload from fake-GitHub / Amnesia C2 host AIDelivery High
Hunts the AmnesiaStealer ClickFix initial-access step where a Terminal-driven shell (zsh/bash/curl) pulls the password-protected ZIP / Mach-O payload from the campaign's counterfeit GitHub page (github.aoitour.com) or the operator host (debug.allllowef.space). Article-specific because it pins on the two named campaign domains rather than generic curl-pipe-shell. Rationale: Pins on the two campaign-specific domains (github.aoitour.com fake-GitHub lure and debug.allllowef.space Amnesia Panel/payload host) confirmed by Jamf and secondary reporting, invoked by a macOS shell — a delivery step that no generic ClickFix rule keys on. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/amnesiastealer-hijacks-chromium.html • https://www.securityweek.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware-steals-data-controls-browser-sessions/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately curling a repo hosted on a lookalike internal mirror (very unlikely with these exact domains)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox with full logging enabled
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling resolving/fetching the IOC domains for analysis
  • A proxy/allowlist test that references the domain string in a benign script comment
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent chain (Terminal.app -> zsh -> curl) and the downloaded artifact path; confirm the target host is one of the two campaign domains and capture the SHA256 of any dropped Mach-O. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the loader and any child Mach-O, and block github.aoitour.com + allllowef.space at proxy/DNS org-wide. 3) Hunt: sweep for the payload hashes (de5748aa..., e853748c...), for outbound WebSocket traffic to allllowef.space (UC C2 rule), and for any headless-browser launches (UC browser rule) on the same host and others that resolved the domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","zsh","dash","osascript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("github.aoitour.com","allllowef.space")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","zsh","dash","osascript")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("github.aoitour.com","allllowef.space")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AmnesiaStealer stream_module: headless Chromium launched with remote-debugging + hardening-off flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the marquee AmnesiaStealer behaviour where the real browser binary is relaunched in headless mode with the exact CDP-abuse flag combo (--headless=old, --remote-debugging-port, --remote-allow-origins=*) against a cloned profile, enabling live operator control of authenticated sessions. The three-flag combination is essentially unique to this abuse and rare in legitimate use. Rationale: Uses the exact flag triad (--headless=old / --remote-debugging-port / --remote-allow-origins=*) that Jamf documents for stream_module; --remote-allow-origins=* on a headless production browser is the discriminator that separates this from benign CI/testing headless Chrome. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/amnesiastealer-hijacks-chromium.html • https://www.securityweek.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware-steals-data-controls-browser-sessions/
ATT&CKT1185 T1539 T1564
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/build agents running headless Chrome for automated UI tests (Puppeteer/Playwright/Selenium) — but these rarely set --remote-allow-origins=*
  • A developer manually debugging a web app with remote DevTools on their own machine
  • Browser-automation RPA tooling that opens a scriptable headless instance
  • Synthetic-monitoring agents (e.g. Datadog/NewRelic browser checks) launching headless Chromium
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node","chromedriver","geckodriver","java","ruby","python3","python3.11","playwright","cypress") and ProcessCommandLine !has "--test-type"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process that launched the headless browser and the --user-data-dir value; a non-browser, unsigned Mach-O parent pointing --user-data-dir at a temp/clone directory is confirmation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the headless browser and its parent, and force-expire the user's web sessions (revoke OAuth/refresh tokens, reset SSO) since authenticated cookies were live-driven. 3) Hunt: pivot on the parent SHA256 across the fleet, look for the same user-data-dir clone path, cookie/Login Data reads, and outbound WebSocket to the relay (C2 rule).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--remote-allow-origins"
| where FileName has_any ("Google Chrome","Microsoft Edge","Brave Browser","Vivaldi","Opera","Chromium","Arc")
     or FolderPath has_any ("/Google Chrome.app/","/Microsoft Edge.app/","/Brave Browser.app/","/Vivaldi.app/","/Opera.app/","/Chromium.app/","/Arc.app/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-debugging-port"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--remote-allow-origins"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("Chrome","Edge","Brave","Vivaldi","Opera","Chromium","Arc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AmnesiaStealer C2/relay egress to Amnesia Panel host (allllowef.space / aoitour.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts the WebSocket relay and payload/upload traffic from an infected Mac to the AmnesiaStealer operator infrastructure (debug.allllowef.space) and the fake-GitHub delivery host (github.aoitour.com). Complements the process rules with a network pivot that also fires if the payload runs before process telemetry is captured. Rationale: debug.allllowef.space is the confirmed operator host serving the bot API, payload archive, upload endpoint and Amnesia Panel; github.aoitour.com is the fake-GitHub lure. Both are hard IOCs corroborated by Jamf, so any resolution/connection is high fidelity. Also matches on the two payload SHA256s. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/amnesiastealer-macos-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1185
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst or sandbox intentionally connecting to the C2 for research
  • Threat-intel/IOC-validation platform (VirusTotal, urlscan) resolving the domain from a corporate egress IP
  • DNS sinkhole or security-tool passive resolution logging the domain
  • Typosquat-monitoring service enumerating lookalike GitHub domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host and process initiated the connection and whether the traffic looks like a persistent WebSocket (long-lived session, small periodic frames ~3fps screencast). 2) Contain: isolate the host, sinkhole/block allllowef.space and github.aoitour.com org-wide, and revoke the affected user's web sessions and keychain-derived credentials. 3) Hunt: search all endpoints that resolved these domains, correlate with headless-browser launches and keychain access on the same hosts, and add the payload SHA256s to blocklists.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("allllowef.space","github.aoitour.com")
   or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in~ ("de5748aac4a4d4cb48cf050652679e6bc49eda33d9ffaa0d280b578122fab55a","e853748ca8f9a5a9168263617409a9039ab09f4ffc7d860374c1e3b0b67b31a5")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("allllowef.space","aoitour.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AmnesiaStealer credential harvest: keychain dump, APFS TCC-bypass mount, and fake password prompt AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts AmnesiaStealer's macOS credential-access primitives: dumping the login keychain via the `security` tool, abusing the mount_apfs TCC bypass (CVE-2020-9771) to read protected data, and prompting the user for their admin password via a hidden-answer osascript dialog. Scoped to non-system parents to keep it stealer-focused. Rationale: Maps to AmnesiaStealer's documented password-capture and keychain-theft chain: the fake admin-password prompt (osascript hidden answer), keychain extraction via `security`, and the CVE-2020-9771 mount_apfs TCC bypass. Restricting parents to non-system paths keeps it aimed at the stealer rather than OS internals. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/amnesia-stealer-macos-infostealer-clickfix/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-infostealer-spread-clickfix/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1056.002 T1006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or MDM script running `security find-generic-password` to retrieve a stored Wi-Fi/service credential legitimately
  • Admin using osascript to prompt for a password in a homegrown IT automation script
  • Backup/imaging tooling mounting APFS snapshots under /System/Volumes/Data
  • Developer tooling (fastlane, keychain CLI helpers) accessing the login keychain during CI on a build Mac
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("fastlane","jamf","munki","security","tccutil") and not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/Library/Apple/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the parent process and its signature/notarization; an unsigned Mach-O parent (or one matching the payload SHA256s) invoking `security dump-keychain` right after an osascript password prompt is a confirmed kill-chain. 2) Contain: isolate the host, assume the login keychain and all stored credentials are compromised — rotate keychain-stored passwords, browser-saved logins, and reset the macOS account password. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host with headless-browser launches and C2 egress (other UCs), and sweep the fleet for the same parent hash and osascript-password-prompt pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "security" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dump-keychain","find-generic-password","find-internet-password"))
     or (FileName =~ "mount_apfs" and ProcessCommandLine has "/System/Volumes/Data")
     or (FileName =~ "osascript" and ProcessCommandLine has "hidden answer" and ProcessCommandLine has "password")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/System/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/libexec/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "security" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dump-keychain","find-generic-password","find-internet-password"))
     or (ActingProcessName has "mount_apfs" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/System/Volumes/Data")
     or (ActingProcessName has "osascript" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "hidden answer" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "password")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
